191.event_title: The Senate censures Senator Joseph McCarthy
191.event: In spring 1954 the Army-McCarthy hearings, carried in full on national television, showed Senator Joseph McCarthy badgering witnesses and ignoring procedure and ordinary courtesy, and the Senate Historical Office records that by June he had greatly damaged his image with the American people. The Senate, which its historians describe as weary of his embarrassing antics, then referred a censure resolution to a bipartisan select committee. On 2 December 1954 it voted 67 to 22 to censure him for his conduct towards two Senate committees, and after the vote he lost his power and standing.
191.explanation: A senator who had dominated the press and the Senate for four years lost his influence once the public had watched him at length and grown tired of him.
191.tie_back: The kural traces a chain from wearying talk to the irritation of the many listeners and then to contempt from everyone, which is close to the path from the televised hearings to the Senate's formal censure.
191._accuracy_note: A strong case of a public speaker exhausting his audience and becoming scorned, though McCarthy's speech was harmful as well as empty, which goes beyond the kural's idle talk.

192.event_title: Khrushchev's intemperate speech at the farewell reception for Gomulka
192.event: At a Kremlin-attended farewell reception in Moscow for the visiting Polish leader Wladyslaw Gomulka, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev turned to the Western diplomats present and delivered a long, boastful, off-the-cuff harangue about the capitalist countries, Hungary and the Suez crisis. TIME reported that by the time he finished, the Western diplomats had left the room. One line from the speech, rendered in English as a declaration that the Soviets would bury the West, became one of the most widely remembered remarks of the Cold War.
192.explanation: Unplanned words spoken before a large gathering of foreign envoys did lasting damage to the speaker's image abroad, far beyond the occasion itself.
192.tie_back: The kural warns that pointless talk before many people does more harm than an unkind act among friends, and Khrushchev's rambling remarks before the diplomatic corps were repeated around the world for decades.
192._accuracy_note: It shows the outsized public cost of careless talk before an assembly, but the kural's specific comparison with wronging friends has no direct counterpart here.

193.event_title: The Tichborne Claimant undone by his own testimony
193.event: A man who came from Australia claiming to be Sir Roger Tichborne, the lost heir to an English baronetcy, sued for the family estates in a civil trial that opened in May 1871 and ran for 102 days. Under a cross-examination by Sir John Coleridge that lasted more than three weeks, his long testimony failed to hold up, and his case collapsed in March 1872 after evidence of tattoos that the real Roger had and he did not. He was then tried for perjury, found to be Arthur Orton, a butcher's son from Wapping, and sentenced on 28 February 1874 to fourteen years' penal servitude.
193.explanation: The claimant's own words, poured out at enormous length in court, were what exposed him.
193.tie_back: The kural says that long talk spread over worthless matter itself announces the speaker's lack of worth, and the claimant's weeks of testimony are what proved him an impostor.
193._accuracy_note: A good illustration of a speaker condemned out of his own mouth, though his talk was deliberate deception rather than mere idle words.

194.event_title: Lysenko's report to the August 1948 session of the Soviet agricultural academy
194.event: At a session of the Lenin All-Union Academy of Agricultural Sciences approved by Joseph Stalin, its president Trofim Lysenko delivered a report denouncing Mendelian genetics and its supporters, and announced that the Communist Party's Central Committee had approved it. After the session, classical genetics was officially condemned, and many scientists working in it were dismissed or moved to other fields. Teaching and research in standard genetics stayed effectively banned in the Soviet Union into the 1960s, and Lysenko is now remembered as a symbol of science corrupted by politics.
194.explanation: Rhetoric with no scientific substance, delivered before a large assembly with state backing, set back a whole field of science and harmed many careers.
194.tie_back: The kural says that graceless words with no benefit, spoken before many, cut a person off from goodness, and Lysenko's speeches put his name to the persecution of honest scientists.
194._accuracy_note: Lysenko's words were worse than merely useless, so the event goes beyond the kural, and his own moral decline is not something the sources describe in those terms.

195.event: Returning from Munich, where Britain, France, Germany and Italy had agreed that Czechoslovakia must give up the Sudetenland to Germany, Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain displayed an Anglo-German declaration signed by himself and Hitler and told the crowd at Downing Street that he believed he had brought back peace for our time. Germany went on to occupy the rest of Czech lands in March 1939 and invaded Poland in September 1939, and Britain declared war. Chamberlain's phrase became a lasting byword for political naivety.
195.explanation: Chamberlain was a respected, hard-working statesman, yet one confident public pronouncement that proved empty did lasting damage to how he is remembered.
195.tie_back: The kural warns that when even people of good character speak empty words, their eminence and honour slip away, and Chamberlain's reputation has never fully recovered from his promise of peace.
195._accuracy_note: A clear case of an honourable figure's reputation spoiled by words that proved hollow, though his words were a sincere misjudgement rather than idle chatter.

196.event: Physicist Alan Sokal of New York University submitted an article titled Transgressing the Boundaries: Towards a Transformative Hermeneutics of Quantum Gravity to the cultural studies journal Social Text, which published it in its spring/summer 1996 issue without any review by a physicist. Shortly afterwards Sokal revealed in the magazine Lingua Franca that the article was a parody, deliberately filled with impressive-sounding jargon and nonsense. The affair set off a worldwide debate about standards of rigour in academic writing.
196.explanation: The hoax showed that language can have all the outward form of learned argument while containing nothing of substance.
196.tie_back: The kural calls the person who shows off empty words the chaff of humanity, grain-shaped but without a kernel, and Sokal's article was built to be exactly such a husk, to show how easily it could pass for the real thing.
196._accuracy_note: The chaff image fits the empty article very well, but Sokal wrote it deliberately to expose empty words, not because he delighted in them.

197.event_title: Ignaz Semmelweis orders doctors to wash their hands
197.event: At the First Obstetrical Clinic of Vienna General Hospital, where women attended by doctors and medical students died of childbed fever far more often than those in the midwives' clinic, the Hungarian physician Ignaz Semmelweis concluded that doctors coming from autopsies were carrying the cause on their hands. In 1847 he required doctors and students to disinfect their hands with a chlorinated lime solution before examining patients, and the death rate fell sharply. His message was unwelcome to many colleagues, his ideas were largely rejected during his lifetime, and he returned to Pest in 1850; they were accepted only after his death.
197.explanation: Semmelweis told his profession something it did not want to hear, and it saved lives wherever it was put into practice.
197.tie_back: The kural allows the worthy to say what is unpleasant but never what is useless, and Semmelweis's unpopular instruction was entirely unpleasant to its hearers and entirely useful.
197._accuracy_note: A very close fit to the kural's ranking of useful but unwelcome speech above pleasant emptiness.

198.event_title: Einstein's short paper on mass and energy
198.event: Albert Einstein, then working at the Swiss patent office in Bern, sent the journal Annalen der Physik a brief follow-up to his paper on special relativity, titled Does the Inertia of a Body Depend Upon Its Energy Content? In only a few pages he argued that a body that gives off energy as radiation loses mass in proportion, the result now written as E = mc squared, although the paper does not set out the equation in that form. It became one of the most consequential short papers in the history of science.
198.explanation: A handful of pages carried an idea that reshaped physics and later underpinned both nuclear energy and our understanding of how stars shine.
198.tie_back: The kural says that those who seek rare and precious benefits speak only words of great benefit, and Einstein's brief paper contained almost nothing but its essential argument.
198._accuracy_note: A good example of economy joined to great value, though it is a single paper rather than a lifelong discipline of speech.

199.date: Weekly, over many years of his public life (died 1948)
199.event: For many years Mohandas Gandhi kept every Monday as a day of silence, during which he did not speak and, when he had to communicate, wrote notes instead, even when a meeting with an official could not be avoided. He kept the practice through the busiest years of the independence struggle and used the day for writing and other work. Gandhi himself allowed only rare exceptions, such as severe pain or comforting someone in distress.
199.explanation: The weekly silence was a deliberate discipline of speech, kept by one of the busiest public figures of his age.
199.tie_back: The kural describes people of clear vision who never utter meaningless words even through heedlessness, and Gandhi's silent Mondays were a regular training in saying nothing that was not needed.
199._accuracy_note: The practice shows restraint of speech, but the kural describes an inner purity that needs no rule, which no outward habit can fully demonstrate.

200.event: In the middle of the Battle of Britain, Prime Minister Winston Churchill issued a War Cabinet memorandum titled Brevity, now held at the UK National Archives as CAB 67/8/11. He asked ministers and officials to make their reports much shorter and to set out the real point concisely. He argued that the time saved would be great and that the discipline of stating the real point briefly would help clearer thinking.
200.explanation: At a moment of national danger, Churchill treated wasted words as a real cost to the war effort.
200.tie_back: The kural's rule is to speak only the words that are useful and never those that are useless, which is almost exactly what Churchill ordered his officials to do.
200._accuracy_note: A very close match to the kural's rule, though Churchill's memo was about written reports rather than speech in general.
